IT RATCHETS BOTH WAYS. An unwaived failure fails the suite; a waiver whose cells now ALL pass also
fails it, so deleting the entry is part of the fix.
THE SCAN-ROUTE CELLS CARRY NO WAIVERS and must stay that way: `policy` and `baseline` are clean on
all four engines. `report/declared` — a well-formed ⟨0.21⟩ manifest — is clean on all four too, which
is the control that makes the two broken triggers below findings about a TRIGGER rather than about
the whole `gate --report` route.
WHAT THE ROUTE x TRIGGER EXTENSION FOUND, and why the two triggers are waived separately.
P5 shipped driving `scan --policy` with an unparseable-source trigger only — and the two cells it
tested were the two already fixed. Adding the `gate --report` route with three report-shaped triggers
put 8 cells red across all four engines, on clauses the spec already states.
EACH ENGINE IMPLEMENTS ONE HALF OF §3.3.1 AND BREAKS THE OTHER, which is the finding worth keeping:
on a MALFORMED manifest rust/ts/swift fail closed (clause 1: exit 2) and DELETE the violation from the
document (clause 2 broken — `violations: []` where the same policy over the same entry gives 1),
while java keeps the violation and does not fail closed at all. Neither behaviour is a subset of the
other, so a fix that simply copies one engine to the others would trade one half for the other.
`count0` is broken FOUR-WAY and is the cheaper fix: SPEC §2 ⟨0.24⟩ already rules that
`analyzed.count == 0` is 'I judged nothing' and MUST NOT read as full coverage, and no engine reads it
on this route. The chained-report form of the same rule is separately waived in
trust-monotonicity-baseline.json (java/swift `empty_zero`), so this is the same defect on a third
surface.

known.why: fails closed (exit 2) but writes `violations: []` — the real `deny Net` hit the same policy finds over the same entry is ABSENT from the artifact. Clause 2 (`a real violation still dominates`) unimplemented on this route; clause 1 correct.
identical to rust: exit 2, `violations: []`, and the refusal document sets neither `incomplete` nor `unanalyzed`, so the refusal is not machine-readable either.
identical to rust and ts. Three engines agreeing here is not evidence they are right — they share the reading that a refusal replaces the verdict rather than riding beside it.

THE OPPOSITE HALF: keeps the violation (exit 1, `violations: 1` — clause 2 correct) but does not fail closed on the malformed manifest at all, so `incomplete_only` exits 0. A present-but-UNREADABLE manifest is not a claim of completeness (§2 ⟨0.24⟩'s denylist rule) and must not be read as one.
`analyzed.count == 0` is 'I judged nothing' (SPEC §2 ⟨0.24⟩) and MUST NOT read as full coverage; the gate exits 0 over it. Four-way — see the note above.
